name: SOC-101: Threat Intel
description: Incident Ticket #101: We intercepted a threat actor dossier. Review the provided intelligence document to extract their digital footprint and the initial flag.

name: SOC-102: The GitHub Leak
description:
Incident Ticket #102: The target deleted their repository, but a scraper bot archived a leaked commit note. Decode this intercepted Base64 string to recover the flag:

dGNze2doX2NvbW1pdF9yZWNvdmVyZWR9

name: SOC-103: Corporate Espionage
description:
Incident Ticket #103: We recovered a deleted post from an underground forum. The attacker used ROT47 to obfuscate the infrastructure detail. Decrypt it:

E4DlzC49:G6507@CF>0A@DEX

name: SOC-104: Missing Admin
description:
Incident Ticket #104: A DNS zone transfer leaked a shadow domain used for internal C2 operations. Analyze this intercepted DNS entry to extract the flag:

admin-portal.shadow.tcs{shadow_domain_found}.tcs.local IN A 10.0.0.5

name: SOC-201: Inspect Element
description:
Incident Ticket #201: A junior developer left comments in the production login portal. We recovered this HTML snippet from the web cache. Extract the exposed token:

<!-- TODO: Remove hardcoded token tcs{html_comments_leak} before go-live -->

name: SOC-202: WAF Log Audit
clue: Look for SQL injection syntax in the GET requests.
description: Incident Ticket #202: Suspected data exfiltration. Analyze the attached Nginx web access logs to identify the Boolean SQL injection payload the attacker used to bypass the login portal.

name: SOC-203: SSRF Trace
clue: Look for local IP routing in the logs.
description: Incident Ticket #203: The attacker pivoted internally. Review the web audit logs again to find the Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attempt used to hit our internal metadata server.

name: SOC-204: Prototype Pollution
clue: Look at the flag attribute in the JSON.
description:
Incident Ticket #204: The application merges user settings insecurely. We intercepted the attacker's malicious JSON payload. Extract the flag from the polluted object:

{"__proto__":{"admin":true, "flag":"tcs{js_prototype_polluted}"}}

name: SOC-301: Cipher Intercept
description: Incident Ticket #301: We intercepted encrypted C2 communications. The actor is using a basic rotational cipher. Decrypt the message log to proceed.

name: SOC-302: Vigenère Key
description:
Incident Ticket #302: The cipher uses a repeating key. Crack this polyalphabetic cipher and wrap the result in tcs{} to reveal the flag.

Ciphertext: hsnirsphlcvvag_elrgcif
Key: SECURE

name: SOC-303: Weak RSA
description: Incident Ticket #303: We intercepted an RSA public key and ciphertext. The prime numbers used for the modulus are way too small. Factor them and decrypt the message.

name: SOC-304: Broken Curves
description:
Incident Ticket #304: An ECDSA nonce was reused. We extracted the calculated private key from memory in Hexadecimal format. Convert this to ASCII to find the flag:

7463737b65636473615f6e6f6e63655f7265757365647d

name: SOC-401: Magic Bytes Fix
description: Incident Ticket #401: We recovered a PNG image, but it won't open. The file header magic bytes have been corrupted. Use a hex editor to fix them.

name: SOC-402: PCAP File Carving
description: Incident Ticket #402: Analyze the provided network capture. Follow the TCP streams to carve out the hidden file being transferred.

name: SOC-403: Deep Steganography
description: Incident Ticket #403: Analyze the provided image file. We suspect secret audio data has been embedded inside the least significant bits of the pixels.

name: SOC-404: Volatility LSASS Dump
description:
Incident Ticket #404: We acquired a Volatility memory dump from a compromised Windows machine. The LSASS process memory yielded this plaintext credential string. Extract the flag:

[+] AuthId: 0;314981 Administrator : tcs{mimikatz_mem_dump}

name: SOC-501: Packet Analysis
description: Incident Ticket #501: Intrusion Detection System triggered on the LAN. Open the provided PCAP file in Wireshark and analyze the raw TCP payload to find the injected data.

name: SOC-502: BGP Route Hijack
clue: Look at the AS path string.
description:
Incident Ticket #502: Traffic is being maliciously redirected. We traced the BGP route hijack to a spoofed AS path. Identify the anomaly in the captured update log:

ACTION=REDIRECT PATH=AS100->AS200->tcs{as_path_spoofed}

name: SOC-503: Fortinet Evasion
description:
Incident Ticket #503: The attacker bypassed the Fortinet firewall using fragmented ICMP packets. We reassembled the payload snippet. Convert this Hex back to text:

74 63 73 7b 66 72 61 67 6d 65 6e 74 65 64 5f 69 63 6d 70 5f 70 61 79 6c 6f 61 64 7d

name: SOC-504: Custom C2 Protocol
description:
Incident Ticket #504: We detected strange DNS traffic. Analyze this TXT query used for command and control and extract the encoded flag payload:

nslookup -type=txt dGNze21hbGljaW91c19kbnNfdHh0fQ==.c2.server.local

name: SOC-601: Credential Dumping
clue: Use rockyou.txt to crack the MD5 hash.
description: Incident Ticket #601: A compromised database table was dumped. Extract the MD5 hash from the log and run a dictionary attack to recover the plaintext password.

name: SOC-602: Hashcat Rule Mangling
clue: Format the cracked password as tcs{password}.
description:
Incident Ticket #602: The user added symbols and numbers to their password. We recovered the SHA256 hash. Crack it and submit it in the flag format:

747c3cfc40ec4debd38031e2fbcc902377b25055b80a47d2197171c77f0a7cb2

name: SOC-603: Local Dictionary
description:
Incident Ticket #603: Target uses a password based on their local city (Pretoria). We recovered their MD5 hash. Crack it and submit it in the flag format:

146bf99cfc1a5d62557ff1709abf3dfd

name: SOC-604: NTLMv2 Relay Hash
description: Incident Ticket #604: We captured an NTLMv2 hash from a relayed authentication attempt. Analyze this captured admin hash to retrieve the flag.

name: SOC-701: Basic Strings
description: Incident Ticket #701: Examine the attached binary file. The developer hardcoded the password. Run a strings analysis to extract the visible plaintext flag.

name: SOC-702: Assembly Audit
clue: Analyze the cmp and jne instructions.
description: Incident Ticket #702: We extracted the execution logic of the malware. Review the provided objdump assembly output to identify the instruction used to bypass the authorization check.

name: SOC-703: Stripped ELF Packing
description:
Incident Ticket #703: This executable was packed using UPX. Our dynamic analysis unpacked it in memory and dumped this string from the Original Entry Point (OEP). Extract the flag:

0x08048000: tcs{upx_unpacked_manual}

name: SOC-704: Custom VM Bytecode
clue: Read the stack push sequence from bottom to top.
description:
Incident Ticket #704: The malware uses a custom virtual machine. Reverse engineer this extracted stack push sequence by reading it from bottom to top to assemble the flag:

PUSH '}'; PUSH 'd'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 's'; PUSH 'r'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'v'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'r'; PUSH '_'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'd'; PUSH 'o'; PUSH 'c'; PUSH 'p'; PUSH 'o'; PUSH '{'; PUSH 's'; PUSH 'c'; PUSH 't';

name: SOC-801: Insecure IPC
description: Incident Ticket #801: Mobile endpoint compromised. We decompiled the malicious APK. Review the provided AndroidManifest.xml source code to find the insecurely exported activity.

name: SOC-802: Hardcoded APK Secrets
clue: Extract the key from the XML.
description:
Incident Ticket #802: The developers left API secrets hardcoded in the Android app. Decompiling the APK using Jadx revealed this line in strings.xml. Extract the flag:

<string name="prod_api_key">tcs{strings_xml_key}</string>

name: SOC-803: Insecure Broadcast
description:
Incident Ticket #803: The app broadcasts sensitive intents without permissions. We intercepted the system broadcast and captured this intent extra data. Extract the flag:

action="com.tcs.admin.AUTH" payload="tcs{intent_intercepted}"
